narrative:
The model estimates an 80% chance that you will leave your current job, which is why your promotion request has been denied. This high probability reflects patterns the system sees in your overall profile compared to others who tend to stay.

Three factors stood out most in driving this prediction toward leaving. First, having received other job opportunities while at your current employer was the strongest influence pushing the model to expect you might depart. Employees predicted to stay rarely report receiving such external offers, so this signal strongly suggested higher turnover risk for you.

Second, your total years of professional experience (6-10 years) also contributed noticeably toward predicting you would leave. While this experience bracket is fairly common among those expected to stay, the model interpreted your specific combination of overall career length and current role as leaning away from long-term retention.

Third, working in the “other” sector (rather than medical or education, which dominate the stayers) added further weight toward expecting departure. This sector shows more variable loyalty patterns than the more stable fields where most retained employees work.

Taken together, these elements created a profile the model associates with higher likelihood of moving on. Your organization should discuss retention strategies with you, such as exploring internal growth paths or addressing any unmet needs that might be making external opportunities attractive. You may also want to reflect on your long-term career goals to see whether staying aligns with them or if a change would better serve your aspirations. (248 words)
